1:
The chapter opens with Moses still inside the cloud, and the reformed John Gill fixes the setting in a line: the word came to him when he was on the mount, in the midst of the cloud with God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers on what that means for the record we have. We may suppose that in forty days among the holy angels who attend the divine Majesty Moses saw and heard very glorious things belonging to the upper world; but they were things which it was neither lawful nor possible to utter, and so in the transactions he set down he says nothing to satisfy the curiosity of those who would intrude into what they have not seen. He writes only what he was to speak to the children of Israel — for scripture is designed to direct us in our duty, not to fill our heads with speculations nor to please our fancies. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same restraint, and Adam Clarke's chapter summary keeps the frame plain: the Lord addresses Moses out of the Divine glory and commands him to speak to the Israelites, that they may give him free-will offerings.

Keil and Delitzsch, reading with grammatical-historical care, state the purpose of everything that follows. The covenant just concluded needed a definite external form, a visible bond of fellowship in which God might manifest himself to the people and they might draw near to him as their God; therefore Jehovah told Moses that Israel were to erect him a sanctuary, that he might dwell in the midst of them. The construction and arrangement were determined in all respects by God himself, who showed Moses a pattern of the dwelling and its furniture and prescribed with great minuteness both the form and the materials of every part. If the sanctuary was to answer its purpose, its erection could not be left to the inventive faculty of any man whatever, but had to proceed from the One who was there to manifest himself as the Holy One in righteousness and grace. The people could only carry out what God appointed — and could fulfil their covenant duty only in the readiness with which they supplied what the work required.

Henry draws out the royal figure. God had chosen Israel to be a peculiar people and would himself be their King; as King he had already given them laws, and now he orders a palace set up among them, here called a sanctuary. Some think that though altars and groves had been used for worship before, no house or temple had ever been built for sacred uses in any nation until this tabernacle, and that the celebrated temples of the heathen took their rise from it. There God kept his court: he manifested his presence, so that with that in the midst of them they might never again ask whether the LORD was among them or not; and because in the wilderness they dwelt in tents, even this palace was ordered to be a tabernacle, that it might move with them — an instance, Henry says, of the condescension of the divine favour. Thither the people must come to consult his oracles and bring their sacrifices, and there all Israel must meet to pay their joint respects.

Both Henry and Wesley then look past the type. The holy places made with hands were figures of the true, as Hebrews 9:24 has it. The gospel church, Henry says, is the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man, and the body of Christ, in and by which he made atonement, was the greater and more perfect tabernacle of Hebrews 9:11. Last of all, the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, as in a tabernacle.
2:
Gill marks the change of audience — the word spoken on the mountain was to be carried down to the camp — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains why the command for materials comes before any description of the building. God, being about to order a dwelling for himself such as the circumstances allowed, prefaced his directions about its form by instructing Moses to invite the people to contribute from their stores the substances suitable for the dwelling and its appurtenances. The erection of sanctuaries, he adds, is one of the fittest occasions for a man to show gratitude by giving God of his own, largely and liberally; and when the time came a noble spirit was not wanting (Exodus 35:21-29).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes up the word itself. The offering is the terumah, a kind of free-will offering consisting of anything needful for the occasion; it properly signifies something lifted up, the heave-offering, because in presenting it to God it was lifted up to be laid on his altar. Clarke sets the transaction in the language of a court: God requires a tent suited in some sort to his dignity, because he was to act as their king and dwell among them, and they were to consider themselves his subjects, bringing presents as a subject does before his prince. Ellicott renders the qualifying clause literally — of every man whose heart impels him — and lays down the principle without softening it: unless gifts come from the heart they are an offence to God, who loves a cheerful giver. Wesley says the same from the other side: it was not prescribed to them what or how much they must give, but left to their generosity, that they might show their good-will to the house of God.

The reformed John Calvin agrees that the tribute is not demanded authoritatively but freely offered, and grounds it in a rule he takes to run through all scripture: no obedience is pleasing to God except what is voluntary. He grants that everything we have is God's already, and that what he bountifully gives is polluted unless we devote it to his glory; yet in his indulgence he permits us the free use of all, if only we testify that it remains under his power. God needed no assistance from a people he was feeding daily with manna, and yet he would have every one, from the least to the greatest, bring something in testimony of their piety. What he then spent on a visible sanctuary he now requires for the building of his spiritual temple: properly speaking he alone builds his Church, yet he uses the work of men and will have many builders associated with him, distributing the gifts of his Spirit in certain measures (1 Corinthians 12:7) so that each may employ what he has received. And this, Calvin says, should be the best incentive of all — that none is so poor or humble but that his offering is acceptable, however small and almost worthless in the eyes of men.

Calvin also uses this verse to argue a question of sequence raised against him: whether the tabernacle was built before Moses brought down the first tables. He answers that it was, gathering it from the tent Moses pitched outside the camp in token of Israel's divorce from God, which he takes for the sanctuary already standing; the later rearing is then a setting of it anew in its proper place, when the covenant was at last deposited in the ark as a pledge. Against him stood the argument that it could not be made before its fashion was shown in the mount — a point Calvin turns to his own side, since the pattern had been shown to Moses before the Law was promulgated and was afterwards only shown again more fully.
3:
Gill takes the list as a menu rather than a levy. Some one or other of these things was to be taken of each man who had a heart to give and the power in his hand; it was not expected that every one should bring something of each kind, but that every man should give, and there be received of him, whatever of these suited him best to bestow. Many of them were abundantly supplied for the service out of what they had brought with them from Egypt, and since it was the LORD who gave them favour in the eyes of the Egyptians and so the riches they carried away, they lay under the greater obligation to part with some of it freely for his service.

Ellicott traces the same wealth with a historian's care. The Israelites had brought out of Egypt both their ancestral property — the possessions of Abraham and the accumulations of Joseph — and the rich gifts pressed on them at the moment of their departure, and they had added to it by the plunder of the Amalekites. So they possessed a considerable store of the precious metals, and there is no difficulty in supposing they furnished the gold the tabernacle needed without seriously impoverishing themselves. He notes that the silver was comparatively small in amount and appears in the end to have been provided in another way, by the half-shekel of the census (Exodus 30:12-16); and that the brass — rather bronze, since brass proper seems to have been unknown at this time — was small in quantity and of no great value, and would have constituted no serious drain on their resources.

Clarke works through the three metals word by word. Zahab, he says, properly signifies wrought gold, what is bright and resplendent, as the word implies; and he distinguishes it from the other terms in the great passage on mining in Job, where gold is named five times under four different words — segor, from a root meaning to shut up, gold still in the mine or shut up in its ore; kethem, from a root meaning to sign or stamp, gold made current by being coined; zahab, wrought and highly polished, probably what was used for overlaying or gilding; and paz, denoting solidity and compactness, gold formed into plate. It is the polished metal that is asked for here, because it was in a state fit to be variously manufactured for the service of the sanctuary. Silver, keseph, he derives from a root meaning to be pale or white, so called from its well-known colour; and brass, nechosheth, he takes for copper, unless the factitious metal commonly called brass is meant, which is formed by combining the ore of zinc with copper. Because it took so fine a polish and kept its lustre, it was used among ancient nations for weapons of war and defensive armour.

Calvin refuses to rank the list. What the poor offer of their little will not be eclipsed by the abundance of the rich, since God deigns to reckon goats' hair among the sacred offerings not less than gold, purple, and precious stones; and by the varied and manifold contributions he would show, as in a glass, that a variety of gifts is necessary to the building of the spiritual temple. The rich did not scruple to have their gold and silver and purple mixed with brass, iron, and other common materials — so those who now aid the edification of the Church by their more excellent gifts should admit poor brethren into fellowship without contempt or dislike.
4:
Three dyes and two fabrics are named, and the witnesses spend their strength on what exactly was being asked for. Gill reports that the Jewish doctors are much divided about the words, some pleading one colour and some another, but that after the labours of Bochart and Braunius the received rendering stands as the most correct. His own point is about the substance rather than the shade: what the people brought was neither the colours themselves, which could not be carried, nor even the materials for dyeing them, but wool or cloth already dyed — Jarchi and Josephus take it of wool so coloured — made up into yarn and woven, and much used afterwards in the garments of the priests, in the curtains, and in the veil between the holy and the most holy place.

Ellicott, working from Egyptian evidence, identifies the three tints closely. The blue was probably a dark blue produced from indigo, which was the only blue known to the Egyptians; the purple a purplish crimson from the murex trunculus, the main source of the Tyrian dye of the ancients; the scarlet a colour furnished by the coccus ilicis, the insect of the holm oak, largely employed in antiquity though now superseded by the brighter tint got from the cochineal of Mexico. What the people were asked to furnish, he judges from the later record of the work, was linen yarn of the three colours. The fine linen he takes for white thread spun from flax, which is found to be the material of almost all Egyptian dresses and mummy cloths — of a yellowish white, soft, and wonderfully fine and delicate. On the last item he is brief and vivid: the covering of an Arab tent is to this day almost always of goats' hair, an excellent fabric being woven from the soft inner hair of the Syrian goat and a coarse one from the animal's outer coat, and it was for the first of the three outer coverings of the tabernacle that this yarn was wanted (Exodus 26:7-14).

Clarke pursues the same words through the classical writers. Techeleth he takes as an azure or sky colour, rendered hyacinth by the Greek and Latin versions, a sky-blue or deep violet. Argaman is a very precious colour extracted from the shell-fish, from which he supposes the famous and costly Tyrian purple came, the manner of its dyeing being largely described by Pliny. Tolaath signifies a worm, of which the colouring matter was made; joined with shani, which carries the sense of repeating or doubling, it implies that to strike the colour the wool or cloth was twice dipped — hence the Vulgate's scarlet twice dyed, and Horace's line about robes that the twice-dyed purple stains. It is the same colour, he adds, that the Arabs call al kermez, whence the French cramoisi and the English crimson. Whether shesh means linen, cotton, or silk is not agreed among interpreters; the rabbins, taking the word for six, suppose it always means the fine linen of Egypt in which six folds made one thread. And of goats' hair Clarke observes that in Asia Minor, Syria, Cilicia and Phrygia the goats carry long, fine, beautiful hair, in some cases almost as fine as silk, sheared at proper times and manufactured into garments; from Virgil he shows that cloth so made was reckoned nearly of equal value with cloth formed from wool. Wesley, content to let the specialists work, says only that these were materials of those colours.
5:
Rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins, and shittim wood: the second of the three has cost the commentators more labour than almost any word in the chapter. Gill notes simply that of the red skins was made a covering for the tent. Ellicott sets them in their region — North Africa has always been celebrated for the best possible leather, Herodotus describes the manufacture of his own times, and to this day the best books are bound in morocco; brilliant colours were always affected by the North African races, and their red skins have been famous in every age. Probably, he thinks, the Israelites brought many such skins out of Egypt.

Clarke reads the phrase more literally still — the skins of red rams — and holds that no dye need be supposed at all. It is a fact attested by many respectable travellers that in the Levant sheep are often met with that have red or violet-coloured fleeces, and almost all ancient writers speak of the same thing: Homer describes the rams of Polyphemus as having a violet-coloured fleece, and Pliny and Aristotle mention the like. From facts of this kind, he suggests, it is very probable that the fable of the golden fleece had its origin; and Virgil's line about the ram that shall change his fleece for a sweetly blushing purple came to his mind when he saw the variously coloured sheep of the Zetland Isles.

On techashim the witnesses genuinely divide. Clarke reports that few terms have afforded greater perplexity, and follows Bochart, who he says has exhausted the subject and seems to have proved that no kind of animal is intended here but a colour. None of the ancient versions acknowledge an animal except the Chaldee, which seems to think of the badger, and from it our own translation is borrowed; the Greek and Latin have skins dyed a violet colour, the Syriac azure, the Arabic black, the Coptic violet. The colour Bochart contends for is the hysginus, a very deep blue, which Pliny describes as crimson dipped again in purple. Keil and Delitzsch take the other road and look for a creature. The seal is not known in the Arabian Gulf, so they prefer the sea-cow found in the Red Sea, whose skin is admirably adapted for sandals; in this animal the upper skin is thicker and coarser than the under, which is only two lines thick and very tough, so that it would serve either for the thick covering of a tent or for the finer ornamental sandals of Ezekiel 16:10, and the Bedouin still make sandals of it. Ellicott agrees that the rendering by badger is a very improbable conjecture, since the badger is native neither to North Africa nor to the Arabian desert; the Arabic word, he says, names a marine animal resembling the seal, or is applied with some vagueness to seals, dugongs, dolphins and dog-fish, and one or more of these is probably meant.

The wood ends the verse quietly. Ellicott states that the shittah is now generally admitted to be a species of acacia, since there are no trees in the Sinaitic region from which boards could be cut except the palm and the acacia; the Sinaitic acacia is a gnarled and thorny tree, in Tristram's phrase somewhat like a solitary hawthorn in its habit of growth but much larger, and though it does not now grow there to a size that would yield the long planks required, it attains that size in Palestine and may formerly have done so in Arabia. Its wood is hard and close-grained, orange with a darker heart, well adapted for cabinet-work. Clarke reports that some suppose the finest species of cedar and others the thorny acacia, which abounds in the very desert where Moses was; Wesley calls it a wood of Egypt and the Arabian deserts, very durable and precious.
6:
Two commodities are asked for here, and both are named before the things that will need them exist. Gill identifies the first without hesitation — oil for the light of the lamps in the candlestick — and follows the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi in taking it for olive oil. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the same brevity, referring the oil forward to the candlestick and glossing the second item as perfumes: spices for the anointing oil, and for the incense, whose Hebrew name means literally the scents, since the materials of which it was compounded were not all of them fragrant.

Ellicott makes the anticipation itself the point of the verse. It is assumed here that the sanctuary about to be commanded will need to be lighted, and oil is therefore to be provided; only later is it laid down that the oil must be pure olive oil, beaten. So too with the spices: the phrase is better read as for the anointing oil, a particular thing taken for granted before it has been described, and there is a like assumption that such oil will be needed and that spices will be a necessary ingredient in it. The need was real enough, for the tabernacle itself, all its vessels, and the priests appointed to serve in it had in the end to be consecrated by anointing, and the particular spices to be mixed were enumerated in their place (Exodus 30:23-24). The last clause he reads in the same way — not sweet incense in general but the sweet incense, the incense which would have to be burnt, whose composition is given afterwards.

Clarke turns from the ritual to the commissariat and raises a difficulty about supply. The oil, he reasons, they must have brought with them from Egypt, for they could get none in the wilderness where there were no olives. But that observation opens a wider one, and he states it as a general caution about this whole body of directions: it is likely that this and some other commands refer more to what was to be done when Israel was in its fixed and settled residence than to what was possible while they were wandering. The spices he treats as no difficulty at all, since the ingredients for a confection of sweet incense abounded in different parts of those countries.

What holds the verse together is that the offering has already begun to look past the tent to the service inside it. The metals, dyes, skins and timber of the preceding verses are the fabric; oil and spices are consumed in the using, and they are asked for before the lamp is designed that will burn the one or the altar built that will smoke with the other. Ellicott's repeated word — assumed — is the honest description: the reader is being told what the sanctuary will require before he is told what the sanctuary is, and the list itself quietly promises the light, the anointing, and the incense that six chapters will go on to describe.
7:
The offering closes with the costliest items, and the witnesses cannot agree what the first of them was. Gill explains the English name from the appearance of the stone — the onyx is so called from its likeness to the nail of a man's finger — and then lays the versions side by side without deciding: the Targum of Onkelos calls them stones of beryl, the Targum of Jonathan gems of beryl, and the Greek version stones of sardius, while some take them for the sardonyx, which has a likeness both to the onyx and to the sardius. Ellicott sets out the same disagreement with the names of its parties: shoham is rendered sard by the Septuagint, sardonyx by the Vulgate and Josephus, and beryl by Rosenmüller and others, while in Job 28:16 the Greek translators give the very same word as onyx. There is thus, he concludes, considerable doubt what stone is meant. Keil and Delitzsch come down, cautiously, for beryls, referring back to the stone named in the rivers of Eden. Clarke, who had met the word there too and acknowledged the difficulty then, will not choose between onyx, sardine and emerald; he offers instead a guess of his own, that it may have been the fine pale Egyptian pebble, several specimens of which a friend had brought him from the coast of the Red Sea.

On the second class of stones there is no dispute. The Hebrew calls them stones of filling, and Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both take that as a technical term for jewels that are set — stones so cut as to be proper to be fixed in the gold work of the breastplate. Ellicott adds the arithmetic, and it is unexpectedly small: only three such stones seem to have been required as offerings for the first class, one for the high priest's breastplate and two for the shoulder-pieces of the ephod, while the stones of the breastplate proper were twelve in number and all different.

Because the ephod is named here for the first time in the chapter, Clarke pauses over it at length, admitting at the outset that it is very difficult to tell what it was or in what form it was made. It was a garment of some kind peculiar to the priests, and ever considered essential to every part of divine worship, for without it no person attempted to inquire of God. Since the root of the word means to tie or bind close, Calmet supposed a kind of girdle, brought from behind the neck and over the shoulders, laid crosswise on the stomach and then carried round the waist so as to gird the tunic; where it crossed on the breast was the square ornament called the breastplate, set with twelve precious stones, each bearing the name of one of the sons of Jacob. There were two sorts, Clarke says: a plain linen ephod for the ordinary priests, of which no particular description is given because there was nothing singular in it, and one very much embroidered for the high priest, composed of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine twisted linen, and fastened on the shoulders with the two engraved stones — which he is careful to distinguish from the stones of the breastplate, with which they have often been confounded. Calmet's account makes it a series of belts fastened to a collar to keep the priest's garments close to his body; Clarke himself inclines to think it was rather like the garment worn by heralds, covering back, breast and belly, open at the sides, joined on the shoulders by a piece of the same stuff, and probably without sleeves. Keil and Delitzsch add the one detail the narrative supplies about how these stones were come by: the precious stones were presented by the princes of the congregation.
8:
Here is the end to which the whole list of gifts has been subordinate. Ellicott states the situation the command answers: hitherto Israel had had no place of worship, no structure dedicated to God, and God now brings that state of things to an end. In Egypt they had seen buildings of vast size and magnificence raised in every city for the Egyptian gods; they are now to have their own holy place, their own house of God. But since they were still nomadic, without fixed abode and continually shifting their quarters, a building in the ordinary sense would have been unsuitable — they must soon have quitted it, or else have foregone their hopes of Palestine. God therefore devised for them a structure in harmony with their condition, a tent-temple modelled on the ordinary form of the better Oriental tents but of the best materials and of an unusual size, and still portable; and this structure, with its contents and adjuncts, occupies the rest of the book.

Gill glosses the noun from the fact — a holy place to dwell in, so called from his dwelling in it — and Clarke, taking the word for the innermost sanctuary the high priest entered once a year, quotes Ainsworth for the reason all the particulars are to be referred here and opened by this. That sanctuary was the place of prayer and of the public service of God; it signified the Church, which is the habitation of God through the Spirit; it was a visible sign of his presence and protection. As the high priest entered the tabernacle and passed through the veil into the most holy place where God dwelt, so Christ entered into the holy of holies, and we also enter through the veil, that is to say his flesh. Clarke reads the sanctuary as a type applied three ways — to the person of Christ, to every Christian whose body is a temple, and to the Church — and takes God's dwelling in the tabernacle for a figure of Christ's dwelling by faith in the hearts of believers (Ephesians 3:17).

Both reformed Calvin and wesleyan-arminian Wesley guard the promise from being taken grossly. Wesley answers in a sentence: not by his essence, which is everywhere, but by his grace and glorious operations. Calvin takes longer because he sees the promise doing double work. God is here setting an inestimable recompense before a people about to be asked to give: no one willingly deprives himself of his own unless he has some compensation in view, so that they may expend cheerfully God promises to dwell among them, than which nothing is more desirable. But we must beware, he says, of imagining anything inconsistent with the nature of God; he who sits above the heavens and whose footstool is the earth could not be enclosed in a tabernacle. Because in his indulgence for the infirmities of an ignorant people he desired to testify the presence of his grace by a visible symbol, the earthly sanctuary is called his dwelling among men — it was not the infinite essence of God, but his name, the record of his name, that dwelt there.

Keil and Delitzsch attach the pattern-clause that follows and defend its tense against a common inference. The words about what is shown in the mount do not prove that Moses had already left the mountain and returned to the camp; the participle does not refer to the past, and the past tense used later of the same seeing is explained simply enough by the sight of the model preceding the description of its parts. Calvin draws the same clause into a rule for the workmen: they were to copy the pattern shown to Moses and not dare to invent anything, since it would be a profanation to mix up anything human with the commands of God.
9:
Nothing in the sanctuary is left to the builders' judgement, and this verse says so before a single measurement is given. Gill puts it in the plainest terms: the sanctuary was to be made in all respects exactly according to the view of it Moses now had upon the mount, and which he was to communicate to the workmen for their instruction and direction. Wesley enlarges the same thought — God showed him an exact plan of it in little, which he must conform to in all points, and did not only show him the model but gave him particular directions for framing every part of it according to that model.

The interesting question is what kind of showing it was, and here the witnesses part. Ellicott sets out the three positions that have been maintained: that God showed Moses a material structure furnished with material objects, as a model to be copied; that he showed him a pictorial representation of the whole; or that he gave him a series of visions in which the forms were presented to the eye of the mind. The entire analogy of the divine dealings, Ellicott judges, is in favour of the last. Clarke leans the other way. He reports the supposition that there had been a tabernacle before the one Moses was to build, though it probably did not now exist, and that the tabernacle Moses is ordered to make was to be formed exactly on the model of that ancient one — the pattern of which God showed him in the mount. He adds the sense of the noun in support: the word signifies literally the dwelling or habitation, and was so called because it was the dwelling place of God, and the only place on earth in which he made himself manifest.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the hinge of the chapter, the general command that the following particulars execute; from here the description turns to the ark, and every later measurement is an instance of this one rule. That is Wesley's point as well, and he draws from the proportions of the narrative itself a lesson about what scripture is for. When Moses was to describe the creation of the world, though it is such a stately and curious fabric, he gave a very short and general account of it; but when he comes to the tabernacle he does it with the greatest niceness and accuracy imaginable — for God's church and instituted religion are more precious to him than all the rest of the world. He that gave us no account of the diameter of the earth or the magnitude of the stars has told us particularly the measure of every board and curtain; and the scriptures were written not to describe to us the works of nature, a general view of which is enough to lead us to the knowledge of the Creator, but to acquaint us with the methods of grace and those things which are purely matters of divine revelation.

Taken together the witnesses agree on the substance while dividing on the mode. Whether the pattern was an object, a picture, or a vision, its function was the same: to put the whole design outside the reach of human invention, so that what Israel built was received rather than devised. Whatsoever is done in God's service, as Wesley sums it, must be done by his direction and not otherwise.
10:
The furniture begins with the ark, and Henry marks the order as significant: the first thing commanded is the furniture of the most holy place and the special token of God's presence, for which the tabernacle was erected to be the receptacle. All the witnesses agree on what the thing itself was — a chest. Gill calls it a coffer to put things into, made of the wood just named; Clarke notes that the Hebrew word covers chest, coffer or coffin, and that this was the most excellent of all the holy things of the Mosaic economy, for whose sake the tabernacle and afterwards the temple were built. Ellicott adds a philological caution that keeps the picture modest: the word here is not the one used of Noah's vessel or the basket of the infant Moses, but a different term, properly a coffer of small dimensions used to hold money or valuables. Sacred coffers, he observes, were important furniture in Egyptian temples, usually holding the image or emblem of some deity and built to be readily carried in processions.

The measurements draw a small disagreement, since the cubit has to be estimated. Henry and Wesley reckon that if the Jewish cubit was three inches longer than our half-yard, twenty-one inches in all, the chest was about fifty-two inches long and thirty-one broad and deep; Clarke, taking the same cubit, gives about four feet five inches by two feet six; Ellicott works with a shorter measure and makes it three feet nine inches long, two feet three broad and deep. Clarke reasons from the dimensions to the tables — since the ark was chiefly intended to hold them, their length was probably not less than four feet and their breadth not less than two — and notes that the depth was meant for other matters besides: Aaron's rod, the pot of manna, and the like, though he thinks these were laid up beside the ark rather than in it.

Henry turns to the name of what was to go inside. The tables are called the testimony because God did in them testify his will; his giving them that law was a token of his favour, and their acceptance of it a token of their subjection, so that the law would be a testimony against them if they transgressed. From that he draws three observations. The tables were carefully preserved in the chest, to teach us to make much of the word of God and hide it in our innermost thoughts, as the ark was placed in the holy of holies; and it intimates the care Providence ever did and ever will take to preserve the records of divine revelation in the church, so that even in the latter days there shall be seen in his temple the ark of his testament (Revelation 11:19). The ark was the chief token of God's presence, which teaches that the first evidence of his favour is the putting of his law in the heart, for God dwells where that rules. And provision was made for carrying it about in all their removals, which intimates that wherever we go we should take our religion along with us.

Gill reads the chest as an eminent type of Christ, and works the figure through the material. The name of a coffer where treasure lies agrees with him, for in him lie the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and all the fulness of grace; and the wood chosen — a wood that does not rot, which the Greek translators render incorruptible — may denote his duration in the natures united in his person: in his divine nature he is God from everlasting to everlasting, and in his human nature he saw no corruption.
11:
Two details are added to the chest, and both raise a question of technique. Gill answers the first flatly: the command is not to gild the ark but to put a plate of pure gold over it. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by weighing what was possible in a desert. It is conceivable, though scarcely probable, that gilding is intended; gilding was well known in Egypt long before the time of Moses, and may have been within the artistic powers of some of the Hebrews. But it is a process requiring much apparatus, and far less likely to have been practised in the wilderness than the simpler expedient of overlaying with gold plates — which would also have been thought more suitable, because more valuable. It is the Jewish tradition, he notes, that plates were employed. The command covers both faces of the wood, within and without, so that the chest was gold to the eye on every side.

The second detail is the crown. Clarke reports the word as meaning a border, and quotes the Greek version's striking rendering — waves of gold wreathed round about — which turns a rim into an ornament. Ellicott takes it as a rim or border carried round the edge of the chest at the top, and offers a reason beyond ornament: its object was probably to keep the mercy seat in place. That reading makes the crown a piece of engineering as well as decoration, a lip to hold the solid gold lid from shifting when the ark was lifted and carried.

Keil and Delitzsch group this verse with the four that follow it as one set of directions for the ark's covering, rings, staves and contents, and gloss the crown in the same way as a golden rim encircling the chest like an ornamental wreath. Their interest runs on to the last item of the set, the testimony that was to be deposited inside — the two tables of stone on which the ten words spoken by God to the whole nation were written, and which Moses had yet to receive from him.

The verse is small, but it sets a pattern the rest of the chapter follows. Nothing is left at the level of a general instruction: the metal is specified, the surfaces it must cover are specified, and the finishing edge is specified, so that the workman has no room left for invention. Ellicott's practical note is the useful one to keep in view — the choice between gilding and plating was not a matter of taste but of what could actually be done in a desert camp, and the answer given here is the one a travelling people could carry out with the gold they had already brought with them out of Egypt.
12:
Having described the chest, the directions turn to the question of how it will travel, and the four verses belong together: rings cast and fixed, poles cut and plated, poles set through the rings, and the poles never to be withdrawn. Gill takes the first step at its most literal — a mould was made and the melted gold poured into it, and so the rings were fashioned — and notes that the poles were made of the same wood as the ark and covered with plates of gold, so that they appeared to be all of gold, the wood not being seen at all. The purpose of the rings, he adds, is disclosed by the next command: they were there to receive the staves.

Ellicott is careful to distinguish this arrangement from what an Egyptian eye would have expected. The ark was not to be carried in procession, as the sacred coffers of Egypt were; but it would have to be carried whenever Israel resumed their journeyings, and the rings were made to receive the two poles by which it would then be borne on the shoulders of the priests. His main contribution is a correction of the English. Where the text speaks of the four corners, the Hebrew says literally at the four feet — the rings were affixed not at the upper corners of the chest but at the bottom ones, so that when the ark was carried on men's shoulders it might be raised above them and be in no danger of coming into contact with the persons of its bearers. He anticipates the obvious objection, that rings set so low would make the load unsteady, and answers it with Kalisch: the smallness of the ark's dimensions rendered its safe transportation, even with the rings at its feet, not impossible.

The command that the poles are never to be taken out draws the most comment, and it draws a real difficulty with it. Gill states the rule twice over — they were not only to be put in but to remain in, and that always. Ellicott gives the reason: the staves were to stay in the rings whether the ark was in motion or at rest, so that there might never at any time be a necessity for touching the ark itself, or even the rings. The stake is not ceremonial fastidiousness but life: he who touched the ark imperilled it, as the man who put out his hand to it found (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Clarke adds a second reason of a different kind — the ark was to be considered as always in readiness to be removed, since God had not told them at what hour he would command them to strike their tents.

Clarke then faces the difficulty squarely. If the staves were never to be taken out, how can it be said in Numbers 4:6 that when the camp should set forward they were to put in the staves, which implies that on encamping they took them out? He reports a reconciliation he thinks carries great show of probability: besides the staves that passed through the rings and were simply the handles by which the ark was lifted, there were two other poles in the form of a bier or handbarrow, on which the ark was laid for the march after it and its own staves — still in their rings — had been wrapped in the coverings of skins and blue cloth. Those bearing poles were what the later passage speaks of; they were drawn out from under the ark whenever the people encamped, while the ark's own staves stayed where they had been put.
16:
The chest is now to be filled, and the witnesses spend the verse on the name of what goes into it. Gill states the plain sense first: this was the principal use of the ark, and by the testimony is meant the law written on the two tables of stone. It is so called, he explains, because it was a testification of the mind and will of God, of what he would have done and what omitted; and since the Israelites had declared their approbation of it and promised obedience, it would stand as a testimony against them should they transgress. Ellicott says the same thing more sharply — the tables were God's witness against sin — and notes that it is from its contents that the chest gets the title it carries through the rest of the Old Testament, the ark of the testimony. Clarke derives the Hebrew word from a root meaning to bear witness to or of a person or thing, and points out that the tables were not yet given when this order was issued; he extends the witness beyond them to everything the ark came to hold, Aaron's rod and the pot of manna and the holy anointing oil, all of which he reads as bearing testimony to the Messiah in his prophetic, priestly and kingly offices.

Calvin presses the title further, and it is the most substantial reading in the verse. The name indicates that something more is contained in the law than the rule of a just and holy life: it is the compact whereby God bound himself to his people and his people to himself, which is why the tables are afterwards called the tables of the covenant instead of the testimony. In this passage and others like it the word is equivalent to a contract, what is commonly called a convention. He supports the breadth of the term from the Psalms, where not only the commandments but whatever God delivered by the hand of Moses for the salvation of his people goes under the name of testimonies; and from the parallel in Psalms 19:7, where testimony is added as if in explanation of law — the law of the LORD is perfect, the testimony of the LORD is sure. So too where the prophet sends his hearers to the law and to the testimony (Isaiah 8:20), it is not that two different things are meant, but that the usefulness of the law is commended, because it contains all that God would have testified to his people.

Gill closes with the figure he has been building since the ark was first described. That the law was laid up inside and preserved there may signify that the law was in the heart of Christ, which he undertook to fulfil and did fulfil with pleasure; that he has become the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believes; and that it remains with him as a rule of walk and conversation for his people, so far as it is of a moral, holy and spiritual nature. The point of the verse, on every reading offered here, is that the covenant document is not displayed but deposited — put out of reach under a lid of solid gold, in the innermost room, where nobody could handle it and everybody was bound by it.
17:
A slab of solid gold is made for the top of the chest, and almost the whole comment is a contest over what to call it. Gill reports both sides without heat. Jarchi and Aben Ezra render the word as covering, for so it properly signifies, and what is meant was no more than a lid for the ark, which was open at the top and which it exactly fitted. Yet because the root in another form means to make atonement, others render it the propitiatory, a rendering the apostle appears to favour; and the Greek version takes both senses at once, calling it the propitiatory covering.

Keil and Delitzsch will not allow the first sense at all. The meaning lid cannot be sustained, they argue, notwithstanding that this object was placed upon the ark and did cover the tables within it, because the verb has no literal sense of covering in either relevant conjugation: in the one it occurs only where Noah is told to pitch his vessel, and in the other only figuratively, of covering up sin or guilt, that is, of making atonement. They treat one passage as decisive — the holy of holies is called the house of the capporeth, which cannot possibly mean the covering-house and must mean the house of atonement. Ellicott names the parties on the other side, Knobel and Gesenius, whose difficulty he takes to be with the idea of expiation itself, and answers by grammar: the noun is formed not from the simple verb meaning to cover but from the intensive form, which never means anything but to expiate sins.

Clarke, who reaches the same conclusion, explains how covering and pardon come to be one idea. By an act of pardon sins are represented as covered, so that they no longer appear in the eye of divine justice to call for punishment, and the offender himself is covered or protected from the stroke of the broken law. He then lists what happened at this spot: the blood of the expiatory sacrifices was sprinkled on it and before it on the great day of atonement; and between the cherubim at its two ends the glory was manifested, whence the frequent saying that he dwells between the cherubim. Because the Greek word for it is applied to Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, Clarke concludes that Christ was the true mercy seat — which is Gill's reading too, that here is the seat of mercy, called in the New Testament the throne of grace.

Calvin holds the metaphor in both hands. He grants the philology on both sides, and does not doubt that Moses alludes to a figurative meaning, for the law requires a covering to conceal our transgressions; probably when Paul and John use their Greek words for propitiation they are both looking back to this figure, since God was propitiated toward believers by the covering of the law. As long as the law stands before God's face it subjects us to his wrath, so the blotting out of guilt must be interposed if God is to be reconciled to us. To read the word as no more than a lid seems to Calvin a tame explanation, given that the cherubim are turned to face it and God promises to give his answers from it; by such honourable distinctions it is exalted above the ark it rests on. Wesley states the settled result in a sentence: this propitiatory covering, as it might well be translated, was a type of Christ the great propitiation, whose satisfaction covers our transgressions. Ellicott adds the one measurable fact behind the theology: this was not wood plated with gold but a solid mass of pure metal, whose weight he reckons at some 750 pounds troy — a lavish outlay meant to show that here the accessories of worship culminated.
18:
Two figures are to rise from the ends of the golden lid, and no one in this chapter claims to know exactly what they looked like. Clarke says so outright: what these were we cannot distinctly say. He reports the common supposition of a creature with four heads and one body, made up of the noblest of their kinds — the lion among wild beasts, the bull among tame, the eagle among birds, and man at the head of all — so that they might be, in Priestley's phrase, the representatives of all nature; but he suspects the term often means simply a figure of any kind, such as was sculptured on stone, engraved on metal, or carved on wood. He also corrects the English of his day: cherub is the singular and cherubim the plural — a point Wesley makes as well.

Gill canvasses the same options, that they were birds, or winged animals such as were never seen, or, as the Jews commonly suppose, young men, or figures of an ox; and he judges their form best discerned from the visions of Ezekiel and of John. Ellicott sets out the modern state of the question. Cherubim had been known before this in one connection only, as the guardians of Eden; they are angels of God, though not all angels are cherubim — they are a select class, very near to God, powerful and resolute, and highly fitted to act as guards. It is probably with that in view that they were set on the mercy seat, guarding the precious deposit of the tables toward which they looked. As to their shape, some hold for winged bulls not unlike the Assyrian, others for something still more composite, like the Egyptian sphinxes or the chimaerae of the Greeks; but the predominant opinion, he reports, is that they were simply human figures with the addition of a pair of wings, resembling the Egyptian figures of Truth so often seen inside the sacred arks.

On the manner of making them the witnesses are one, and it matters more than the shape. Ellicott glosses beaten work as not cast but brought into shape by the hammer, and observes that the Hebrew says literally from the two ends — the figures rise out of either end of the lid. Keil and Delitzsch make the consequence explicit: they were made out of the capporeth itself, forming one whole with it and inseparable from it.

What the figures signify divides the witnesses more than what they resembled. Wesley takes them for an emblem of the angelical nature rather than an effigy of an angel, and reads their posture as attendance upon the Redeemer, readiness to do his will, and desire to look into the mysteries of the gospel. Calvin, satisfied that it is enough to know the images were winged and represented angels, says God appointed angels — the ministers of his blessings, by whom he exercises his dominion — to be a symbol of his presence, which is why David and the prophets encourage themselves in prayer by speaking of him as dwelling between the cherubim. Their outstretched wings, he adds, were not meant to hide the lid but to mark the readiness of their obedience, and their turning to face one another shows the harmony in which angels perform God's commands. He records the old allegory that the two figures are the two Testaments, surrounding the mercy seat because Christ is their common object, and calls it a plausible conceit that vanishes before the contradiction of many passages. Gill also rejects the two-Testaments reading, and declines to identify the figures with the angels, since they are distinguished from them; he takes them rather for the saints of both dispensations, the legal and the evangelical, signified by the number two and made of gold to mark their worth in the esteem of Christ.
19:
The placing and the posture of the two figures are settled next, and the first concern is that nobody should misread the arrangement. Gill notes with Jarchi that the situation is spelled out lest it be thought there were two cherubim at each end; there was one at the one end and one at the other, set opposite each other, and both pointing toward the mercy seat between them. Ellicott repeats the point of manufacture that governs everything else here: they were not to be detached images, made separately and afterwards fastened on, but formed out of the same mass of gold as the seat itself, part and parcel of it.

The wings come next, and the witnesses describe them with unusual precision. Gill observes that this command settles the question of their form — they were winged creatures, like the seraphim of Isaiah's vision and the living creatures seen by Ezekiel and John — and notes that the wings did not hang down at their sides but were stretched upward, above their heads. Ellicott has them elevated and advanced at once, so as to overshadow the seat and, as it were, protect it; he contrasts the Egyptian figures of Truth, in which only one wing takes this position while the other is depressed and falls behind the figure. Keil and Delitzsch put the effect in a single word: the wings were to be spread so as to form a screen above the golden lid.

Then the faces. They are turned toward one another, and at the same time toward the seat — bent downward, in Ellicott's reading, as though gazing on it. Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the two directions by having the figures incline or stoop toward the capporeth while facing each other, and they point ahead for the reason: it is over that lid, from between the two cherubim, that God will present himself to Moses and speak with him. The whole arrangement is designed around a spot of empty air.

Gill, as often in this chapter, reads the arrangement as well as describes it. The two set at opposite ends and both pointing inward express for him the situation and office of the ministers of the word under each dispensation, so placed that they derive all their gifts and graces from Christ and point him out to men as the only way of salvation, the only propitiation for sin. The upstretched wings he takes for the readiness and swiftness of those ministers to do the will of Christ, and for their expectation of every supply of grace from him. Whether or not the figure is pressed that far, the physical description leaves an impression the witnesses agree on: two guards of beaten gold, inseparable from the place of atonement they overshadow, with their faces bent toward it and their wings meeting above it, waiting on a voice.
21:
The lid is now to be laid on the chest, and the testimony placed inside it — an order of assembly that Gill treats as the theological heart of the whole design. The mercy seat goes above the ark, as a covering for it; and since the law was what lay in the ark, that arrangement signifies that there is no mercy except in a way of righteousness, no pardon that does not satisfy the law of God and stand consistent with its honour. Mercy is not laid alongside the law here, nor set against it: it is laid over it, and covers what is underneath.

Gill then reads the finished structure from top to bottom. The cherubim above the mercy seat make a throne for the majesty of God, in which he sat; the ark below is a kind of footstool. Christ, the mercy seat and propitiatory, therefore stands between God and his law, and is the mediator between God and men who have transgressed that law. By fulfilling it he has covered the sins of his people, which are violations of it; and being above it, having magnified it and made it honourable, he is able to suppress its charges and accusations and to secure those who are his from its curse and condemnation. The image controls the doctrine: the law is not destroyed by being covered, and the covering is not a concealment but a satisfaction laid on top of it.

Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the closing instruction of the section on the ark, gathering the chest, its contents and its golden covering into a single completed piece before the description passes on. Two things are commanded in one breath — the covering set above, and the testimony deposited within — and the second is repeated from the earlier order, so that the reader is left in no doubt that the tables are inside when the lid goes on. The place where God will meet Moses is therefore also the place where the covenant document is sealed away.

What the verse settles, in other words, is a relation rather than a measurement. Nothing new is built here; the pieces already described are put in their places, and the putting is the point. The document that accuses lies underneath; the gold that atones lies over it; the guards of beaten gold lean toward the gold that atones. Every later thing said about this spot — the sprinkled blood on the day of atonement, the voice from between the cherubim, the title ark of the testimony — depends on the arrangement given here in a single sentence.
22:
The purpose of everything built so far is stated at last, and it is a meeting. Gill takes the promise to run beyond Moses: God would meet with him, and so with the high priest in later times when he entered the holy of holies, and with the people of God as represented by that priest when he went in to inquire of the LORD for them. Clarke fixes the place with precision — over the mercy seat, between the cherubim — and says that in this place God chose to give the most especial manifestations of himself; here the divine glory was to be seen, and here Moses was to come to consult the LORD about the management of the people.

Ellicott names what stood there and explains how the meeting worked. The place of the Shechinah, the visible manifestation of God's presence, was to be between the two cherubim over the mercy seat, and there God would meet his people to speak to them. That speaking, he says, took two forms: literal, as when the LORD answered the inquiries of the high priest by Urim and Thummim; and spiritual, as when he accepted incense, and the blood of offerings, and prayers offered to him by the people through their appointed representatives. And this, Ellicott insists, was the purpose for which the entire tabernacle was designed — which is why its ordinary name in the Hebrew is the Tent of Meeting, a title he thinks the Authorised Version renders unhappily by the tabernacle of the congregation.

Clarke draws the promise inward through a comment of Ainsworth's. The rabbins say that the heart of a man may be likened to God's sanctuary; for as in the sanctuary the divine glory dwelt, because there were the ark, the tables and the cherubim, so in the heart of man it is fitting that a place be made for the divine Majesty to dwell in, and that it be his holy of holies. Clarke calls this a doctrine most implicitly taught by the apostles, and observes that the necessity of having the heart made a habitation of God through the Spirit is strongly and frequently insisted on through the whole of the New Testament.

Read against the rest of the chapter the verse changes the character of the furniture behind it. The chest, the plating, the rings and poles, the solid lid and the two figures are not ornaments of a shrine but the apparatus of a conversation: God appoints a spot, a few inches of air above a slab of gold and between two bent faces, and undertakes to be found there with everything he will command concerning the children of Israel. All that Israel must do is build to the pattern and come.
23:
With the ark finished the directions move out of the innermost room, and Henry marks the change of address carefully: this table was to stand not in the holy of holies — nothing was in that but the ark with its appurtenances — but in the outer part of the tabernacle called the sanctuary or holy place. Gill agrees, setting it on the north side, opposite the lampstand, and gives the reason for it in a sentence: since the sanctuary was a house for God to dwell in, he would have the proper furniture of a house. Ellicott adds only that no other timber was to be used, either for the sanctuary itself or for anything in it.

Clarke develops that domestic logic at length, borrowing from Cudworth and from the Jewish commentator Nachmanides, whose compressed saying he admires: the mystery of the tabernacle was that it should be a place for the Divine habitation to be fixed in — which Clarke takes as a type of God's dwelling afterwards in the human nature of Christ. Since the tabernacle was a house for God to dwell in visibly, everything belonging to a house must be found there. Hence in the holy place a table and a lampstand, because that was the ordinary furniture of a room; the table must have its dishes and spoons and bowls and covers, though they were never used, and must always be furnished with bread; the lamps must burn continually; a fire must be kept always on the altar as the focus of the house; and provision must be constantly brought in, in the sacrifices partly consumed on the altar and partly eaten by the priests, who were God's family and were therefore to be maintained by him. Clarke notes that the altar is actually called God's table and the sacrifice his meat by the prophet (Malachi 1:12), and that salt was strictly commanded in every oblation — because, in Nachmanides' blunt phrase, it was not honourable that God's meat should be unsavoury.

Henry works the same figure from the royal end. The tabernacle being God's house, in which he was pleased to say he would dwell among them, he would show that he kept a good house; and in a royal palace it was fit there should be a royal table. It was to be always spread and furnished with the shewbread, twelve loaves set in two rows, six in a row, one for each tribe, which some make represent the tribes themselves, set before God as his people and the corn of his floor. Henry puts the two chief pieces of furniture side by side to striking effect — as the ark signified God's being present with them, so the twelve loaves signified their being presented to God.

The bread is then read three ways. It was a thankful acknowledgment of God's goodness in giving them their daily bread, manna in the wilderness where he prepared a table for them and the corn of the land in Canaan, so that they owned their dependence on Providence not only for the corn in the field but for the bread in their houses. It was a token of communion: this bread on God's table being made of the same corn as the bread on their own, God and Israel did as it were eat together, as a pledge of friendship and fellowship. And it was a type of the spiritual provision made in the church by the gospel for all who are made priests to our God — in our Father's house there is bread enough and to spare, a loaf for every tribe. Gill reads it the same way and looks further forward still, to the table Christ has in his kingdom, where his saints shall eat and drink with him.
24:
The table is to be plated like the ark, and Gill draws the same lesson from the same operation: it was covered with a plate of gold so that the wood was not seen. He reads the covering as a figure, and hesitates between two applications — it may denote the excellency of Christ's human nature, pure and spotless and adorned with the grace of the Spirit without measure, or rather of his divine nature, which is said to be as the most fine gold, for in him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.

Ellicott explains why this piece in particular deserved the best materials. Like the ark, and like the altar of incense afterwards, the table was to be overlaid with plates of gold; and it was itself a species of altar, since offerings to God lay upon it, and it stood close to the divine Presence. The crown he takes as a border or edging of gold, and here he differs a little from the reading given to the ark's crown: this one had a practical purpose of its own, to prevent what was placed on the table from readily falling off. A rim round the top of a table that must be carried on men's shoulders through a wilderness is not decoration only.

Keil and Delitzsch, who treat this verse and the five that follow as one block of instructions, describe the table's frame with more precision than the English suggests. Besides the golden wreath round the top there was to be a finish, a border of a hand-breadth in depth, surrounding and enclosing the four sides; upon this the top of the table was laid, and into its four corners the feet were fixed. On that account the table was not a simple slab on legs but a framed box of woodwork, plated throughout, with the leaves of its construction hidden under gold. They note too that the vessels which follow — the deep plates in which the shewbread was both brought to the table and set upon it — cannot have been small, since the corresponding silver dishes given by the princes of the tribes were of considerable weight.

Taken with what precedes it, the verse quietly repeats the pattern already set for the ark: acacia frame, gold within the reach of every eye, and a finishing rim. The repetition is not accidental. Two pieces of furniture stand in two different rooms, one holding the covenant document and the other holding bread, and both are built to the same specification out of the same materials — so that a worshipper who was never allowed past the veil could still know that the table he did not see and the table he did were made by one hand and to one design.
25:
A hand's breadth of framing is added, with a second golden edging of its own, and where exactly it sat is disputed. Gill reports the division through Jarchi: some of the Jewish teachers place the border above, running round the top of the table; others place it below, fixed from foot to foot at the four corners, with the board of the table laid upon it.

Ellicott judges the second view nearer the truth and prefers to translate the word as a band or framing rather than a border. He appeals to the one piece of evidence that shows the object rather than describing it — the table carved on the Arch of Titus at Rome, which gives the best idea of the thing. There the band appears as a flat bar about midway between the top of the table and its feet, connecting the four legs and so keeping them in place: a stretcher, in a joiner's language, rather than a moulding. Its golden crown, he adds, can have been only for ornament.

So the two readings differ in what they make the piece do. On Jarchi's first alternative it is a raised lip round the tabletop, of a piece with the crown already commanded; on the reading Ellicott takes from the Roman relief it is structural, the frame that holds a portable table rigid. What both agree on is that the addition was small — a hand's breadth — and that it was finished, like every other edge in this chapter, with gold.
26:
The table is to travel, and the fittings for its journey are given in three quick strokes: four rings, their position, and the poles that pass through them. Gill treats each as a deliberate echo of the ark. The rings are as the ark had, and for the same use as those were, though whether cast, as the ark's were, is not said; and the poles are made in like manner as the staves for the ark, and of the same wood.

Ellicott presses the parallel further and marks where it breaks. The table, like the ark, would have to be carried from place to place; and though it was less sacred than the ark, provision was still made for carrying it by rings and staves. Here too he corrects the English on the same point he corrected it before: the phrase about the four corners is better rendered as the corners that are at the four feet — not the top corners of the table but the bottom ones, so that when it was carried it would be raised above the shoulders of the bearers. And once again he appeals to the Arch of Titus, where the table is shown borne exactly so.

The middle command is the obscure one, and Ellicott says so rather than smoothing it over. The rings are to be over against the border, which he would translate opposite the band or framing; and the meaning, he admits, is not very clear. Had the framing been down at the bottom of the legs, one could understand the rings as fixed opposite the places where the framing was let into them. But the framing appears to have run halfway up the legs, while the rings were at the bottom, so that they could only have been opposite the framing in a loose and vague sense. Gill records the same difficulty from the other end: the ancient versions render the preposition as under the border rather than over against it, while Jarchi has the rings fixed to the feet, over against the top of the border. Ellicott's last note is smaller and firmer — the rings are places for staves, not places of the staves, a receptacle prepared before the poles that will fill it.

What the three verses together establish is an arrangement designed so that nothing consecrated need be handled. The table stands on its four feet in the holy place; when the camp moves, poles already plated with gold slide through rings already fixed at the feet, and the whole is lifted without a hand touching the gold that the bread has lain on.
29:
The table's plate is listed in four Hebrew words, and every one of them is contested. Gill begins with the dishes, on which the loaves were set, and reports Jarchi's curious detail that they were made to the shape of the bread and came in two kinds — one of gold and one of iron. In the iron one the bread was baked, and when it was drawn from the oven it was moved into the golden one until the morning after the sabbath, when it was set in order upon the table.

Clarke works through the whole list with a lexicon at his elbow, and reaches a rather different picture. The first word he takes for the deep bowls in which they kneaded the mass out of which the shewbread was made. The second, commonly Englished as spoons, he argues were censers on which incense was put up — a conclusion he draws from the long inventory of the tribal offerings in Numbers 7:14, where the same word recurs and the vessel is always described as filled with incense. The third, the covers, he supposes a large cup or tankard in which pure wine was kept on the table beside the bread, for the libations poured out before the LORD every sabbath when the old bread was removed and the new laid on. The fourth he derives from a root meaning to clear away or empty, and reports Calmet's guess that these were either the sieves with which the Levites cleansed the wheat — for it is asserted that the grain for the shewbread was sowed, reaped, ground, sifted, kneaded and baked by the Levites themselves — or else the ovens in which the bread was baked; while others suppose they were the vessels dipped into the wine-cup to take out the wine for the libations.

Ellicott agrees with Clarke on one item and differs on the rest, and his evidence is again the sculptured table at Rome. The dishes he takes for large bowls in which the loaves or cakes were brought to the table, such bowls being common in the Egyptian wall decorations. The so-called spoons he agrees were small pots in which the incense was put and burnt, and he notes that two such appeared upon the table on the Arch of Titus. But the covers and bowls he identifies as flagons and chalices to hold the drink offerings which were the necessary accompaniment of every meat offering; and on the last clause of the verse he corrects the translation outright — the phrase rendered to cover withal should be, as the margin has it, to pour out withal, since drink offerings were poured out in libation.

Beneath the disagreement the shape of the service is clear enough on every reading. Bread was carried in and set out; incense stood beside it and was burnt; wine was kept there and poured; and every vessel used at any stage was to be of pure gold. The furniture of God's house, as the earlier verses put it, was to be complete down to the last utensil, whether or not a worshipper outside the holy place would ever see one of them.
30:
Everything so far has been carpentry and goldsmith's work; this verse says what the table was for. Gill sets out the practice: twelve cakes in two rows, which stood a whole week and were renewed every sabbath, the old loaves being eaten by the priests as the new ones were set, so that bread was always there. The Hebrew name he renders bread of faces, because the loaves were always before the face of God. Ellicott gives the same literal rendering — bread of the presence — and sends the reader to the detailed account of the arrangement in Leviticus 24:5-9.

Clarke weighs two explanations of that name and prefers the second. It may be that the loaves were so called because they were made square, in the form of cubes, each side presenting the same appearance, as the Jews will have it; but the Hebrew seems rather to intimate that they were bread of faces because, as the LORD himself says here, they were set before his face. He adds the detail that on the top of each row stood a golden dish of frankincense, which was burnt before the LORD as a memorial at the end of the week when the loaves were changed and the priests took the old ones for their domestic use. Then he does something rare among commentators and stops. It is more difficult, he says, to ascertain the use of these loaves, or what they represented, than almost any other emblem in the whole Jewish economy; many have conjectured, and he feels no disposition to increase their number. The most rational thing he has met with is the observation quoted earlier in the chapter, that the tabernacle was God's house and in it he had his table, his bread, his wine and his lamp, to show Israel that he had taken up his dwelling among them.

Keil and Delitzsch venture the interpretation Clarke declines, and are careful about which way the gift runs. The loaves lay continually before Jehovah as a meat-offering presented by the children of Israel — not as food for Jehovah, but as a symbol of the spiritual food which Israel was to prepare, and a figurative representation of the calling it had received from God. On that reading the bread and the wine standing beside it on the table, being the fruit of the labour Israel bestowed on the soil of its inheritance, were a symbol of its spiritual labour in the kingdom of God, the vineyard of its Lord.

Gill reads the same arrangement two ways at once. Toward God it was a memorial of his goodness in daily providing bread for Israel, presented to him as a thankful acknowledgment, and the very bread they ate at their own tables; and since the priests afterwards ate it, it expressed the communion between God and them, they being his guests and feeding on the same provisions. Toward the church it is typical: the loaves are the people of God, who are all one bread; the cakes being pure and unleavened denotes their purity, simplicity and sincerity, without the leaven of malice and wickedness; and the number twelve stands for the tribes, the whole spiritual Israel of God.
31:
The last piece of furniture in the holy place is the lampstand, and Gill begins with the practical fact that governs the rest: it was a useful piece of household furniture, especially in a house where there are no windows — as there were none in the tabernacle. It stood on the south side, opposite the table. Ellicott corrects two of the English terms before anything is built on them: the bowls, knops and flowers are better rendered cups, pomegranates and blossoms, the cups being afterwards described as like almonds; and the whole was to be of beaten work, as the cherubim were, all of one piece with stem and branches rather than separate ornaments put together.

Keil and Delitzsch itemise the anatomy from the ground up. From the base — the word means the loins, from which the feet proceed, and here the pedestal on which the candelabrum stood — there rose the reed, the hollow stem; and on it were set the cups resembling the calix of a flower, the knobs in a spherical shape, and the flowers, ornaments in the form of buds. Every one of these was to issue from the stand itself so as to form one whole. Clarke describes the finished object as it is generally conceived — one shaft with six branches, adorned at equal distances with flowers like lilies and with bowls and knops placed alternately, a lamp on each branch and one on the top of the shaft, seven in all.

Clarke then makes a claim about this piece that he makes about almost nothing else: we are not so certain of the precise form of any utensil of the sanctuary as we are of this, the golden table and the two silver trumpets. His reason is a monument. After the fall of Jerusalem, Titus carried the lampstand, the table, the trumpets and the book of the law in triumph to Rome, and at the foot of the Palatine the ruins of an arch still carry that triumph in sculpture, the lampstand and the table and the trumpets cut on the panel of the inner wall. Clarke had a model of the arch before him as he wrote, and notes that the carved lampstand is less ornamented than in many engravings and scarcely three feet high. To see these sacred articles gracing a heathen emperor's triumph, he says, affords melancholy reflections; but they had accomplished the end for which they were instituted, since the true light was come and the ever-during bread had been sent from heaven.

The lamp is the one piece of furniture every witness reads symbolically. Henry finds it magnificent, convenient — contrived both to scatter the light and to keep the tabernacle clean of smoke and snuff — and significant. All the light of that house was candle-light, which intimates the comparative darkness of that dispensation while the Sun of righteousness had not yet risen; yet God left not himself without witness, for the commandment was a lamp and the law a light, and the prophets were branches from that lamp. The church is still dark in comparison with what it will be in heaven; but the word of God is the candlestick, a light shining in a dark place. Gill takes the stand for the church, which has no light of its own but what Christ puts into it. Calvin reads the seven lamps as the one Spirit's many gifts, and warns against pressing the number: some have invented a mystery in it, whence the common notion of a sevenfold grace, which is refuted by the longer list Paul gives (1 Corinthians 12:7-11). He takes seven for perfection instead — as if God declared that nothing would be wanting for the full enlightenment of believers who seek it from its one and only source.
32:
The branches are described next, and then what grows on them. Gill notes that the six came out of the trunk or shaft, being beaten out of it; Keil and Delitzsch place them symmetrically, three on either side of the upright stem in the middle. On each branch there were to be three cups made like almonds, with a knop and a flower.

What those three ornaments were is a matter of some care. Gill takes the cups as almond nuts in form, and reports two opinions about their use: either they held oil for the lamps, or, as others think, they caught the snuff that fell from them. The knop, by the signification of the word, was in the form of a pomegranate, and the flower is rendered a lily by the Targum of Jonathan — both of which, Gill observes, are in scripture emblems of the saints endowed with the gifts and graces of the Spirit. Ellicott would translate the first word as cups like almond blossoms rather than nuts, and confesses that it is not quite clear whether the three ornaments ran consecutively along the branch or whether each cup held a pomegranate on which a blossom followed; on the whole he judges Reland's representation to accord best with the latter view. He also corrects the article — it should be another branch rather than the other, since the ornamentation was the same in the first, the second and all the rest; though he suspects that in the longer branches the triple series was probably repeated more often than in the short.

Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to settle a grammatical dispute with consequences for the shape of the whole. Because the words for knob and flower follow the words for cups without a conjunction, Knobel and Thenius took them as explanatory apposition, so that the flower-cups themselves consisted of knobs with flowers bursting out of them. Keil and Delitzsch reject this on two grounds. There is the singular idea of calling a knob with a flower issuing from it a flower-cup at all; and, decisively, the opening verse of the description mentions cups, knobs and flowers in connection with the base and stem as three separate things. If they are three there, they are three here.

The distinction matters because it fixes how much ornament the lampstand carried. On the rejected reading the branches bore three composite blossoms apiece; on the reading Keil and Delitzsch defend, and which the later verses about the shaft support, each branch carried three cups with their knobs and their flowers, and the central stem more still. Either way the design is botanical rather than architectural: a stem, arms curving up from it, and almond blossom at intervals along every one of them, the whole beaten out of a single mass of gold.
34:
Attention moves from the arms to the central stem, and then to the junctions where the two meet. Gill states the difference plainly: the four cups are in the trunk or body of the lampstand, the branches having only three apiece, but this being larger it had four.
