Ellicott makes the reference explicit — by the candlestick in this place must be meant the central shaft, viewed as the thing to which all the rest is accessory — and observes that here the triple series of cup, pomegranate and blossom was repeated four times over.

The knops under the branches are then commanded three times in identical words, and Gill explains why the repetition is not accidental: it signifies that there should be such a knop under each of the three branches on the one side and each of the three on the other. He reports Jarchi's account of what the knop did there — that from the middle of it, which was shaped like a pomegranate or, as others say, like an apple, two branches were drawn out, one to either side; and he passes on the Jewish tradition preserved in the same place that the height of the lampstand was eighteen hands' breadths.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the same joint in the language of a draughtsman. At the point where each of the three pairs of side pipes branched off from the main stem a knob was to be so placed that the arms proceeded from the knob, or from the stem immediately above it. The final command — that the knobs and branches be of the stand itself, all one beaten work of pure gold — lets them assemble the whole from the parts. Upon the vase, they conclude, there rose an upright central pipe, from which three side pipes branched out one above another on either side and curved upward in the form of quadrants until they reached the level of the central stem. On that stem a cup with its knob and blossom was introduced four separate times, so placed that there was a knob wherever the side pipes branched off, immediately below the branches, with the fourth higher up between the topmost pair and the end of the stem; and as there were four such on the main stem, so there were three on each of the arms.

Gill's last note is the shortest in this stretch of the chapter and carries the point of it. The knops and the branches were to be of the same — the same metal, gold, and of the same mass. Nothing in this object was assembled. The pedestal, the stem, the six arms, the cups with their pomegranates and blossoms, and the knobs at every junction were all raised with the hammer out of one piece of gold, so that a lampstand of this size and this intricacy had not a single joint anywhere in it.
37:
The lamps themselves come last, with the small implements that kept them burning. Gill counts them off: six stood on the tops of the six branches and the seventh on the top of the shaft that ran up the middle, and there is no doubt that these were made of gold like the rest. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew word-order is worth preserving — thou shalt make its lamps seven — so that each branch, as well as the stem, was to have its own; and from the Arch of Titus he describes their shape as hemispherical bowls. The lamps were to be lit so as to give light over against the stand, throwing their light forward rather than scattering it.

Two utensils follow, and both concern the wick. Keil and Delitzsch identify the first as tongs, that is, snuffers, and the second as snuff-dishes, dishes to receive the snuff when it is taken from the wicks; they note that elsewhere the same word means an ash-pan, a vessel used for carrying away coal from the fire. Ellicott says the same in practical terms: pincers were needed for trimming the wicks and removing the loose portions, and the dishes for receiving the fragments so removed.

Gill collects the Jewish opinions and finds more variety than one would expect over a pair of tongs. Jarchi took the first instrument for a sort of fork with which they lifted the wicks out of the oil and set them in place; others take them simply for snuffers, though Gill observes that snuffers appear to be distinguished from tongs. For the dishes Jarchi has a sort of small cup in which they put the ash of the lamp morning by morning, when they trimmed away the burnt remains of the wicks that had burned through the night and gone out. Ben Gersom and Lyra offer something more ingenious — that the dishes were vessels full of water, into which the snuffings were dropped so that they should not make a smoke; and Gill, who is not usually generous to speculation, allows that this is not improbable.

It is a small passage and an unglamorous one, and that is its interest. The command that began with a talent of beaten gold and blossoms of almond ends with a pair of pincers and a dish for the burnt ends of wicks — because a lamp that burns from evening to morning every night of the year needs trimming, and the tools that trim it were to be made of pure gold like everything else in the room. Gill reads the seven lights themselves for the gifts and graces of the Spirit, or else for the ministers of the gospel who are the lights of the world; but even on that reading the snuffers keep their place in the inventory.
39:
A weight is put on the whole work, and it is the only measurement the lampstand is given. Keil and Delitzsch note that the talent was to cover not the stand alone but all its vessels — everything belonging to it — and observe that from such a quantity of gold it was possible to make a lampstand of very considerable size. The dimensions are nowhere stated in the Old Testament; they pass on Bähr's conjecture that it matched the height of the table of shewbread, a cubit and a half in height and the same across, or a cubit and a half between the two outside lamps.

The witnesses then try to say what a talent was worth, and their answers are a lesson in how hard such conversions are. Gill reports from Jarchi and Ben Melech that the common talent weighed sixty pounds while the sacred talent was double, at a hundred and twenty, and gives Bishop Cumberland's valuation of a talent of gold at just over five thousand pounds of the money of his day. Clarke works from the same authority but by a longer road, and arrives elsewhere. Taking a talent at three thousand shekels, he reasons from the half-shekel each Israelite paid and the census total to show that a hundred talents came to three hundred thousand shekels; then, reckoning a shekel of the sanctuary at three shillings and gold at fifteen times the value of silver, he makes a talent of gold six thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds sterling, and with the odd shekels added a total above seven thousand pounds laid out on this one piece of furniture and its utensils. Ellicott, writing later, reports the estimates as still unsettled: there are various reckonings of the weight and value of the Hebrew gold talent, but none of them places it much below four thousand pounds, and some carry it as high as ten or eleven thousand.

Clarke draws a conclusion from his own arithmetic that reaches beyond it. It is no wonder, he says, that Titus should have thought this object of sufficient consequence to be one of the articles employed to grace his triumph. But the intrinsic worth of these things was a matter of no consequence to the One whose are the silver and the gold; they had accomplished the end for which they were instituted, and once the glorious person they typified had appeared they were of no further use either in the kingdom of providence or in the kingdom of grace.

Ellicott adds one grammatical note in passing that is easy to miss. The verse says he shall make it, not thou, and the pronoun refers to the artificer by whom the lampstand would actually be constructed — a hint, in the middle of a chapter addressed throughout to Moses, of the craftsmen who would be named later. Keil and Delitzsch, meanwhile, take the signification of a seven-armed stand to be plain from its purpose: to carry seven lamps, trimmed and filled with oil every morning and lighted every evening, so that the house was never dark from dusk to dawn.
40:
The chapter closes where it began, with the pattern shown in the mount, and Clarke reads the placing of the command carefully. This verse is an order given after the tabernacle and its furniture had been described — as if God had said: when thou comest to make all the things I have already described to thee, and the other matters of which I shall afterwards treat, see that thou make everything according to the pattern which thou didst see in the mount. He notes that the Greek version uses the word for a type or form, and thinks Paul had this command in view when he charged Timothy to hold fast the form of sound words he had heard of him (2 Timothy 1:13). The parallel is deliberate: the tabernacle was a type of the Church of God, built on the foundation of the prophets and apostles with Jesus Christ the chief cornerstone, so that as God gave the plan for the tent, he gives the doctrines by which the Church is to be modelled.

Gill takes the charge as addressed to a supervisor rather than a workman — see that they are made by the workmen employed — and states the negative all the witnesses agree on: everything was described in the model, and nothing was left to the will, the humour or the fancy of men. Henry draws two consequences. All God's providences are exactly according to his counsels, and the copy never varies from the original; infinite Wisdom never changes its measures, and whatever is purposed shall undoubtedly be performed. And all his ordinances must be administered according to his institutions — which he takes for the same charge Christ laid on his disciples when he told them to observe all things whatsoever he had commanded them (Matthew 28:20).

Calvin guards the command from being flattened into an instruction about ornament. It is certain, he says, that it is not any mere vision that is in question here, but that the external ornaments of the sanctuary have their spiritual object, as is plain from the explanations given by Stephen and by the writer to the Hebrews. We need not wonder, then, that Zechariah should say God would make manifest under the reign of Christ that what he set before his people under the Law was no empty spectacle.

Clarke ends with a long observation about the borrowing of nations. He holds that the heathen took their best things from divine revelation, and often imitated it closely: their temples had a porch, a nave, an inner sanctuary and an innermost recess where the mysteries were kept, answering to the divisions of this house; they had portable temples, of which the silver shrines for Diana at Ephesus were one kind (Acts 19:24); and they had sacred chests carried in procession as the ark was borne — Plutarch describes the priests of Osiris carrying forth such a chest with a small golden boat in it, and Tacitus tells of a covered vehicle in a northern grove that only the priests might touch, drawn by cows, while war ceased in every district it visited. Since the ancients also hung many-lamped candlesticks in their temples — Pliny mentions one shaped like a tree with lamps for fruit, given by Alexander to Apollo — Clarke supposes these too were copied from the golden lampstand. From the solemnity of the charge he concludes what part of the forty days on the mountain were for: God showed Moses a model of the whole and its furniture, and receiving instruction about it was one part of his employment there. The house resembled a dwelling-house down to its furniture because it was a dwelling; and as the glory was manifested between the cherubim in it, so God was in Christ, in whom dwelt all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
